newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic invites OSCE to check Serbian elections.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic invites OSCE to check Serbian elections.

text.p: Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic on Friday offered to let international experts assess the fairness of disputed elections which have sparked weeks of street protests.

In a letter answering criticisms by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Milosevic invited a delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) "to visit our country and be informed truthfully".

The full text of Milosevic's response, which claimed that opposition charges of socialist vote-rigging had created a "distorted picture" internationally, was published on the front pages of Belgrade newspapers together with Christopher's letter.
The United States has led Western attacks on Milosevic's refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections in Serbia on November 17.
The authorities overturned the results in Belgrade and other towns claimed by the opposition, citing unspecified "irregularities".

The conflict has provoked a wave of peaceful demonstrations that have drawn up to 150,000 people a day onto the streets of Belgrade. There have been reports of some protesters being detained and beaten.
Christopher's letter called on Milosevic to "ensure that the will of your people, as expressed through their votes, is respected and that a dialogue which promotes democratic evolution is opened.
"As you know, manipulation of the electoral results has set back much of the progress made over the last year in improvement of our bilateral relations."
Milosevic rejected the allegations of electoral fraud.
"Democracy in Serbia has a long tradition ... I consider our (electoral) system to be very good," he wrote to Christopher.
The president's assertions contrasted with a report by the independent Humanitarian Law Centre, which concluded that Serbia's electoral legislation was "defective".
The centre alleged that courts which ruled on the dispute, including the Supreme Court, disregarded evidence and failed to explain their reasons for disqualifying Zajedno councillors.
The centre said the supreme court annulled all 92 appeals by Zajedno and upheld only one which was made by the socialists.

Milosevic accused the opposition of undemocratic activities including "vandalism, threats of poltical terrorism, taking children and youth on to the streets and blocking city life in the centre of Belgrade."
